about.title: About the Church Family Tree
about.description: What the Church Family Tree is: a free map of church history, with {{traditionCount}} church traditions and the councils, people and stories that shaped them.

sections.heading: What the tree is
paragraphs: The Church Family Tree is a free, interactive map of church history. It runs from the first house-churches, around 70 CE, to about 2010.
Each family of churches is drawn as a river. The rivers wind, widen and divide as the centuries pass.

sections.heading: What you'll find
paragraphs: The tree maps {{traditionCount}} church traditions, and the councils, people and stories that shaped them. It shows how they connect: which grew out of which, which influenced or argued with each other, and where they broke apart.
The traditions flow in {{riverCount}} rivers across {{eraCount}} eras. Every tradition, council and person has its own page.
A river grows wider when more traditions in that family were active. Its width does not show how many people belonged.

sections.heading: Listen as you explore
paragraphs: Many cards have a short spoken brief, read by a synthesized voice.
New here? A short guided tour shows how the map works.

sections.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs: Every link between traditions names its sources and says how sure the record is. Quotations are checked word for word against the original text.
The tree has been checked with AI tools. Review by church history experts is planned as funding and partnerships allow.
The [method page](method.html) explains how the tree is made. The [data and citation page](data.html) shows how to cite it and download its data.

sections.heading: Who makes it
paragraphs: Faithways Studio, Inc., a Colorado public benefit corporation, makes the tree. It is free to use. Contributions from the people who use it support its work. [Help us grow](support.html).
The same team makes Church in Conversation at churchinconversation.com. You can access Church in Conversation from a growing number of Christian traditions on the tree.
Use of the tree and its data is covered by our [license](license.html).
Questions or ideas? Write to info@churchinconversation.com.

method.title: How the tree is made
method.description: How the Church Family Tree draws, sources, checks and grades each link between Christian movements.

sections.heading: Checked by AI, not yet by scholars
paragraphs: Every claim and every link on the tree has been checked by AI models against the sources, working to our written method. None of it has yet been reviewed by an independent scholar.
When that review happens, the release will say which parts were reviewed and by whom. Academic review is the project's biggest need. The [data and citation page](data.html#review) says how to help.

sections.heading: The narrated briefs
paragraphs: Every narrated brief on the tree is read by a synthesized voice, made with the ElevenLabs text-to-speech service. No person recorded it.
The voice reads the same words the card shows under "Read the brief". Only the spelling of some names is changed for the voice, so that it says them correctly.

sections.heading: How a link is made
paragraphs: A link starts in a movement's own text. Each movement's page tells its story and names the movements it touched.
Every relationship that text names becomes a link. If the sources cannot support it, the text drops it or says plainly that it is uncertain.
An AI model drafts each link. It gives the link a kind, a grade, a short note and its sources.
Most sources are old texts kept as files in the project's library. A quoted source names its file and the exact lines.
A script then checks every quotation, word for word, against that file. A quotation that does not match fails, and so does its link.
Next, a second AI model reviews the work on its own. It is given the data and the sources, not the first model's reasoning. It checks each kind, grade, note and quotation.
The review runs both ways. Every relationship in the text must have its link, and every link must match the text.
Work that fails goes back for changes, for at most three rounds of review. Anything still open after the third round goes to the project lead to decide.

sections.heading: Seven kinds of link
paragraphs: Each link reads as a sentence: one movement, the kind of link, then the other movement. There are seven kinds.

terms.text: The second movement grew out of the first. Its people, communities or institutions came from the first one.
The same community, carried on into a later movement on the tree. This is often the same church in a later age, or under a new name.
Ideas, texts or practices passed from the first movement to the second. This can happen with or without contact between them.
The first movement wrote or acted against the second, by name. The arrow points away from the critic. When both sides wrote against each other, the tree draws two links.
A break that both sides recorded. It runs both ways, so it has no arrow.
A recorded meeting, letter or shared event. It claims no influence. Living at the same time is not enough to count as contact.
A church that joined a council or fellowship of churches, on that body's own record. The arrow points from the member to the council. Membership claims no descent and no influence.

sections.heading: Direct descendants and influence
paragraphs: A tradition's card and page start with its direct line. Descended from lists the traditions it grew out of or continues. Direct descendants lists the traditions it gave rise to or continued as.
That is one step, not every later descendant. Follow the next tradition to go further down the line.

Everything else sits under Influence, argument and contact: ideas that passed, arguments, meetings and memberships. An influence is not a descent. One tradition can shape another without being its parent.
A break sits in its own group, Broke with, because a split is not a continuation. It has no direction, as above.

Only traditions are in these groups. A person, a story or a council belongs to a tradition and shows on its card. Where no direct parent or descendant is recorded, the page says so. That is true of 107 of the 350 traditions.

sections.heading: Five grades of confidence
paragraphs: Each link has a grade. The grade says how sure the record is of the link itself, not of the events its note mentions. A council that names a group can document an argument, for example. It does not, by itself, show that one movement grew out of another.

terms.text: A primary source, written at the time or by the people involved, shows the link itself. Its words are quoted and checked against the file. If that text is not in the library, the link cannot be Documented.
A primary source shows the facts underneath the link, and modern scholars broadly agree on what they mean. The link names at least one of those modern works.
The leading account modern scholars have pieced together from the evidence. The link names the works it comes from.
Scholars disagree. The link gives sources for each side, and its note says what the disagreement is.
The evidence is thin, and the note says so. The link names what little it rests on.

sections.heading: Reading confidence at a glance
paragraphs: On the map, a line's color shows the kind of link, and its pattern shows the grade.

terms.text: Documented.
Widely Accepted, or Dominant Modern Reconstruction. These two grades share the same long dashes, so the name on the card tells them apart.
Contested.
Inferential-Thin.
Gave rise to, or continued as.
Influenced.
Argued against, or broke with. An argued-against line has a small open arrowhead at the end it points to, away from the critic. A break has a small open ring at both ends.
In contact with.

after: Point at a line, or tap it, to read the link with its grade spelled out.
A dotted gold thread joins a movement to the one it continues as in another river. Point at it, too, to see that link's grade.
Every movement's card on the map, and every movement's page, lists its links. Each link there shows its grade by name.

sections.heading: Major links
paragraphs: The map opens with no lines. Under Connections, the Major links switch draws only the major ones.
Three kinds of link are always major: gave rise to, continued as and broke with. They trace lineage and recorded breaks.

Any other link is major only when its own sources show an act of authority. That can be a council, canon, synod or law that condemned or shut out a group or its teaching. It can also be any authority, church or state, removing a bishop or other church head from office.
It can also be a split into a separate church, or a rule or settlement that an authority changed. Such a link carries one sentence on that lasting result, drawn from its sources.
A teaching or book that passed from one side to the other does not, by itself, make a link major.
Minor links are not hidden for good. Every link stays on its movement's card and page. Pick a movement on the map to see all of its links.

sections.heading: What the tree does not claim
paragraphs: A link claims only what its kind says. "In contact with" claims no influence. "Influenced" claims no shared community.
Two movements alive at the same time are not linked for that reason alone.
A river's width shows how many recorded movements in that family were active at the time. It does not measure membership or size.
Each movement's page also tells its story. Some sentences there give well-known background facts that are not yet tied to a source in the library. The links carry the quoted evidence.
No grade on the tree has yet been confirmed by an independent scholar.

sections.heading: Where the history ends
paragraphs: The map runs to about 2010. Traditions that began after that will be added once enough time has passed.
Nothing after 2010 is mapped yet.

sections.heading: What the living mark means
paragraphs: A living mark means one thing: the tradition is alive today, in 2026. It is the only statement the tree makes about the present. Everything else on an entry is history.

The mark belongs to the tradition, not to the entry's dates. An entry that ends in 1300 still carries it when the church, religious order or community it describes survives today. Its later history belongs to a later entry. Where the tree has no later entry yet, the gap is named, and the dates are never stretched to cover it.
An episode counts. A revival, a reform or a single period in a church's history is marked living when the wider tradition it belongs to is still alive.

Surviving ideas are not enough. A school, a party or a sect whose own community ended is not marked living, even when its writings are still widely read. A modern group that adopts an ancient name is not counted as its heir unless a record shows an unbroken community.
Decline is not an ending. A tradition is marked ended only when the record shows a clear end: it dissolved, it merged into another body, or its last member died.

Each mark rests on dated evidence, beginning with the body's own recent words: a dated statement, report or rule. A mark is "documented" when an independent source confirms it and we have checked that source. It is "reported" when it rests on the body's own word, or on an outside source we have not yet checked. Where we hold no dated source yet, the record says so, and the missing source is listed as wanted.
We describe what a body's dated documents say, never what its members believe. A living church can change its teaching, so each mark is a dated reading of the record, not a permanent verdict.
Sometimes two churches claim the same ancestors, or the record breaks off for centuries. Then the claim of descent gets its own confidence grade, on the same five levels the tree uses for links.

sections.heading: What is still to come
paragraphs: Links are built one era at a time. Each era ships as its own numbered release of the data.

The tenth era, {{latestEraTitle}} ({{latestEraDates}}), is not yet linked, because its traditions are still being built. Its movements stay on the map, but the full set of their links is not yet drawn.
Today the tree holds {{linkCount}} links among {{movementCount}} movements.

data.title: Data and citation
data.description: The Church Family Tree's public data file, its current release, its permanent IDs and how to cite it.

sections.heading: The current release
paragraphs: All of the tree's data sits in one public file. The current file is release {{releaseNumber}}, dated {{releaseDate}}.
It holds {{movementCount}} movements and {{linkCount}} links. Each release has a number and a date, so a citation can name the exact version it used.

sections.heading: Download the data
paragraphs: The same file sits at two addresses. Neither one sends you on to another address, so a script can fetch it straight away.
https://www.churchfamilytree.com/data/world-census.json
https://churchinconversation.com/data/world-census.json
The names that search accepts besides the tree's own, each with the line that shows it, sit in a second file with the same release number.
https://www.churchfamilytree.com/data/search-names.json

sections.heading: IDs that never change
paragraphs: Every movement and every link has an ID. Once we publish an ID, we never change it or use it again.
If a link is removed or merged, its ID moves to a retired list in the file. That list gives the date, the reason and any replacement.
If a movement is renamed, its old address leads to the new page. If two entries turn out to tell the same story, one is retired into the other, and its old address leads to the page that took it in.
Each movement page's earlier address, on churchinconversation.com, still works. It sends you, in one step, to the same page here.

sections.heading: Movements and people
paragraphs: Most entries are movements. Some are people: someone the sources treat as a party in their own right, with writing of their own or a recorded position, who founded no lasting movement. In the file, a person entry has the kind "person".

A person entry names the tradition whose story tells it, in the field toldWithin. For a person who belongs to no single tradition, that field is empty. Each movement lists its people, in date order, in the field people.
A link that is about one person names that person in the field concerns. It does so only where the link’s own note or sources name them.

sections.heading: How far each entry is checked
paragraphs: Each entry says how far it has been checked, in the field reviewStatus. "AI-checked" means it was checked with AI tools. "partner-contributed" means it was written with a church partner from the tradition. "scholar-reviewed" means a scholar has reviewed it.
Today every entry is AI-checked. Each movement page says so near its foot.

sections.heading: How to cite the tree
paragraphs: Name the release you used. These examples use real IDs and the current release.

citations.label: The tree
citations.text: From the Church Family Tree by Faithways Studio, Inc., release {{releaseNumber}} ({{releaseDate}}), CC BY-NC 4.0. https://www.churchfamilytree.com

citations.label: A movement
citations.text: “{{exampleMovementName}}.” Church Family Tree, Faithways Studio, Inc., release {{releaseNumber}} ({{releaseDate}}). https://www.churchfamilytree.com/tree/{{exampleMovementId}}

citations.label: A link
citations.text: “{{exampleLinkSentence}}” ({{exampleLinkGrade}}). Church Family Tree, Faithways Studio, Inc., release {{releaseNumber}} ({{releaseDate}}), link {{exampleLinkId}}. https://www.churchfamilytree.com/tree/{{exampleLinkPage}}#{{exampleLinkId}}

citations.label: A release of the data
citations.text: Faithways Studio, Inc. Church Family Tree data, release {{releaseNumber}} ({{releaseDate}}). CC BY-NC 4.0. https://www.churchfamilytree.com/data/world-census.json

after: A movement's ID is the last part of its page address. A link's ID joins the IDs of its two movements with two hyphens. A second link between the same pair ends in --2.
A link's address is either movement's page, then # and the link's ID. It opens the page at that link.

sections.heading: License
paragraphs: Our data and our writing are free to reuse for non-commercial purposes, with credit. The license is CC BY-NC 4.0, from Creative Commons. The [Faithways Studio license policy](license.html) gives the full terms.
Churches, ministries and scholars can do more under our Ministry and Scholarship Permission. To ask for it, fill in the short request form: https://tally.so/r/kb97Br

sections.heading: Help review the tree
paragraphs: Our data has been checked by AI, but not yet by scholars. Academic review is the project's biggest need.
If you teach or research church history, theology or the early sources, we would like to hear from you. Write to info@churchinconversation.com.
The [license policy](license.html#partnerships) explains how review works.
To report an error, use the "Report a problem" button on any page, or write to the same address.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.description: The Church Family Tree sets no cookies and has no accounts. How we count visits without identifying anyone.

sections.heading: In short
paragraphs: The Church Family Tree has no accounts and sets no cookies. We never ask who you are, and nothing we count identifies you.

sections.heading: What we count
paragraphs: Cloudflare hosts the site. We use its cookie-free Web Analytics and its traffic figures to count visits.
The map also counts how it is used: which cards are opened, which briefs are played and for how long, which suggested next step is taken, and time spent on the map.
To tell new visitors from returning ones, your browser keeps a small note of when you last visited.

sections.heading: Turning counting off
paragraphs: Open the map with ?count=off at the end of the address, and the map stops counting your use in that browser. Use ?count=on to turn it back on. Cloudflare's visit totals are not affected.

sections.heading: What stays on your device
paragraphs: The map remembers your settings, such as which parts of the map are showing and your listening choices. They stay in your browser and are never sent to us. Clearing your browser's site data removes them, along with the last-visit note.

sections.heading: Feedback
paragraphs: "This helped" sends only the name of the page. A report or a message sends the page and what you wrote. It includes your first name or email only if you choose to give one. We use feedback to improve the tree.

sections.heading: Other services
paragraphs: Typefaces load from Google Fonts, so your browser asks Google for them when a page opens.
Contributions are paid on Stripe's own pages. Stripe holds your name, email and payment details. We never see your card details.
A link to Church in Conversation tells that site only that you came from the Church Family Tree.

sections.heading: Questions
paragraphs: Faithways Studio, Inc., a Colorado public benefit corporation, runs the Church Family Tree and is responsible for this data. Write to info@churchinconversation.com with questions, or to ask us to delete a report you sent.

support.title: Help us grow
support.description: The Church Family Tree is free for everyone. How you can help it grow: a gift, an introduction to a scholar, a correction or a share.

sections.heading: Their story, in their own words
paragraphs: For two thousand years, people have followed Jesus across vastly different worlds and cultures. Every tradition on this map is built from their own letters, treatises, confessions, life stories, and trusted sources.
Please help us accurately tell their story, so others can see a fuller picture of Jesus and His work through history.

sections.heading: What your support pays for
list: Primary-source research that traces each link back to verified editions
Scholarly review by historians and specialists across traditions
Audio narration, so the story can be heard as well as read
Translations, so people around the world can read it in their own language
Hosting and infrastructure that keeps the service fast and online
The people who research, write, and maintain the platform
after: Published by Faithways Studio, Inc., a Colorado public benefit corporation. Payments are voluntary support for our research and publishing services, not charitable donations. They are not tax-deductible.

sections.heading: Ways to help that cost nothing
list: Introduce us to a scholar, seminary, or professor who might review a section of the map.
Spot a mistake? Use the "Report a problem" button on any page.
Share the map with a pastor, study group, or friend who would find it useful.

terms.title: Terms of Use
terms.description: The terms for using the Church Family Tree and Church in Conversation, in plain words.

sections.heading: In short
paragraphs: You are welcome here. Read, learn and share freely. Please don't copy our sites in bulk or use them to train AI. Our work can contain mistakes, so check what matters to you, and tell us what we got wrong.

sections.heading: Who we are
paragraphs: Faithways Studio, Inc., a Colorado public benefit corporation, makes the Church Family Tree and Church in Conversation. These terms cover both sites. By using them, you agree to these terms.

sections.heading: Using our work
paragraphs: Reading, studying and sharing are free. Our [license policy](license.html) explains everything else you may do with our data, writing and recordings.
Please don't:
list: copy our sites in bulk with automated tools (the full data is offered as one file on our [data page](data.html))
use our sites or data to train AI, unless we have agreed in writing
try to break or overload our sites
present our work as yours, or as approved by us or any church

sections.heading: Voluntary support
paragraphs: Voluntary support pays for the research, scholarly review, narration, translation, hosting and people behind our work. It is not a charitable donation, and it doesn't buy access or any say over our content. It is not tax-deductible. If you ask within 30 days, we'll refund your payment.

sections.heading: The fine print
list: Our sites are for learning, not pastoral, spiritual or professional advice.
We work hard to be accurate, and every claim shows its sources and confidence. Still, our work can contain mistakes.
We offer our sites as they are, and can't promise they will always be available.
As far as the law allows, we aren't responsible for losses from using our sites.
Other sites we link to have their own terms.
Colorado law applies to these terms.
We may update these terms. This version is dated November 12, 2026.
Our [privacy page](privacy.html) says what we keep and why.
